record.title: Financial LLM trading-agent review reports disclosed gaps in shock resilience and security controls
record.summary: The arXiv v1 paper introduces FARSIGHT, a codebook-based method for reviewing published financial LLM trading-agent schemes across market-shock robustness and security controls. It is a scheme-level expert-review framework, not an automated benchmark suite or a live test of deployed agents. Applying it to 15 selected academic schemes, the authors report that 80% lacked evidence for at least one core robustness metric and 100% had at least one security weakness under their codebook. In a five-agent comparison, the LLM-based evaluator disagreed with human ratings on 24/45 metric cells (53.3%) and performed poorly on some newly defined threats. The ratings reflect what papers document, not confirmed absence from implementations; no proprietary production agents or live market behavior were evaluated.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent recoding of the 15 papers or reproduction of the rubric ratings was conducted.
The sample consists of 15 selected academic schemes, not proprietary production agents; a low rating means the paper did not evidence a control and does not prove code-level absence.
The LLM evaluator disagreed with human ratings on 24/45 cells in the five-agent sample and performed poorly on newly defined threats, limiting automation of fine-grained review.

brief.importance_rationale: If the findings generalize, financial-agent research and procurement would need to treat source integrity, deterministic risk controls and compromised-agent containment as core design requirements; however, the study scores disclosed academic schemes rather than deployed systems, so the prevalence and market consequences are unmeasured.
limitations: Single arXiv v1 systematization paper; ratings are author-applied and were not independently recoded.
The final set contains 15 selected academic schemes identified from a literature search ending March 2026; it does not represent proprietary financial agents or establish deployment prevalence.

FARSIGHT is a paper-evidence codebook and expert-review method, not a fixed benchmark suite or live penetration test. A low score indicates that a paper did not evidence a control; the control may exist in code or later versions.

An LLM-based evaluator disagreed with human ratings on 24/45 cells (53.3%) in a five-agent subsample and had errors up to 100% on some new threat types; automated rubric scoring is not a substitute for human review.
Attack scenarios and systemic-risk implications are literature-grounded or simulated; no live market incident, actual financial loss or adversarial broker-in-the-loop exploit was demonstrated.

It is a scheme-level expert-review framework, not an automated benchmark suite or a live test of deployed agents. Applying it to 15 selected academic schemes, the authors report that 80% lacked evidence for at least one core robustness metric and 100% had at least one security weakness under their codebook. In a five-agent comparison, the LLM-based evaluator disagreed with human ratings on 24/45 metric cells (53.3%) and performed poorly on some newly defined threats. technical.claimed_result: Authors report that a literature-grounded FARSIGHT codebook identifies disclosed robustness and security-control gaps across 15 selected academic financial-agent schemes: 80% lack evidence for at least one core robustness metric and 100% have at least one security weakness under that rubric. The method scores evidence in papers, not running systems.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected arXiv v1 paper defines the codebook, selection process, ratings and author-reported LLM-vs-human comparison. No independent recoding or live test of a financial agent was performed.
technical.mechanism: FARSIGHT applies evidence-anchored checklist indicators to published scheme descriptions across four robustness dimensions and three security threat groups: information-source attacks, agent logic/tool/memory attacks, and compromised agents acting as attackers.
technical.regime: Literature search and screening yielded 15 distinct academic financial LLM trading-agent schemes from papers available through March 2026; no inaccessible proprietary systems or live market agents were evaluated. LLM-vs-human scoring used five schemes and 45 metric cells.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper compares human expert codebook ratings with a ChatGPT Deep Research evaluation on a five-agent subsample. Human paper review is the reference for that comparison, but independent inter-team recoding was not conducted.

brief.title: Financial LLM trading-agent review reports disclosed gaps in shock resilience and security controls
brief.why_it_matters: Financial agents can combine external data ingestion, model reasoning and trade execution, so failures in input provenance or deterministic risk controls may affect real capital and interact through markets. The paper offers a structured way to inspect those risks, while its results apply to disclosed academic schemes and do not establish conditions in proprietary deployments.
